articles.headline: Treasury Yields Dip Below 5% as Investors Flee AI Debt for Safety of Government Debt
articles.dek: The 10-year yield ended the week at 4.99% as tech borrowing worries sent money into bonds, even with oil near $100 and the Fed leaning toward a hike.
articles.catch_up: Weeks after 10- and 30-year Treasury yields hit their highest levels in more than 20 years, they have eased as tech stocks sold off over the huge debt that AI companies are taking on to build data centers. The Fed meets next week with rates at 3.75% to 4.00%.
articles.why_it_matters: The 10-year yield is used to price mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt, so its direction shapes what ordinary borrowers pay. Markets still expect a Fed rate hike in December, so relief from falling yields may be short-lived.
body: The yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury note finished the week at 4.99%, up 3 basis points on Friday but still slightly under 5% after dropping below that level Thursday for the first time in a month, CNBC reported. Investors had been selling tech stocks and buying government bonds. In other words, the safest asset available is a loan to a government running large deficits, which tells you something about the alternatives.

Translation: a basis point is 0.01%, and bond yields move opposite to prices. When people rush to buy Treasurys, prices rise and yields fall. Yields are falling this week because nervous investors want somewhere to put money, not because anyone has become more optimistic.

The nervousness has a specific source: the hundreds of billions of dollars tech companies are spending on AI networks, much of it borrowed. CNBC reported that tech stocks sank, yields on outstanding tech bonds rose, and credit default swap spreads widened for a number of AI companies. Translation: a credit default swap is insurance against a borrower failing to repay, and a wider spread means the insurance is getting more expensive.

CoreWeave is the week's showcase. The stock fell 10% on Thursday and 38% in October. Its 9.75% bond due in 2031 now yields 15.72%, and the spread on its five-year credit default swaps is 1,138, above the 1,000 level generally considered distressed. The company is, by the market's own pricing, being treated as a borrower who needs to be asked about collateral.

Bond investors also had other things to ignore. BMO's credit strategy team noted that Treasurys rallied even as WTI crude tested $100 a barrel, which would normally push yields up through inflation worries. WTI futures rose nearly 3% to $102.39 on Friday and Brent gained 2.5% to $115.94, after fresh attacks by Iran-backed Houthi militants on Saudi oil installations. Reports this week suggested the U.S. and Israel could resume strikes on Iran after the Nov. 3 midterm elections. Weakness in French government bonds added to the appetite for U.S. debt.

The economic data was not recessionary. The S&P Global manufacturing PMI came in at 56 against an expected 55.3, the highest in 53 months. Translation: a PMI above 50 means factories are expanding. Meanwhile, the University of Michigan consumer sentiment index was 48, down 0.1 point from September, beating the 46.3 consensus but still down 10.4% from a year ago. One-year inflation expectations rose to 4.7% and five-year expectations to 3.5%.

That mix explains the Fed's position. It is not expected to change rates next week, but CME's FedWatch tool put the probability of a quarter-point hike in December at 70%. Byron Anderson of Laffer Tengler Investments said a sustained bond rally is hard to see unless the narrative flips to recession, and noted that we are far from that, with two hikes still priced in. BMO said a sustained deterioration in financial conditions could alter the Fed's calculus.

Official data point to the same tension. The latest figures showed the 10-year at 5.13% on Oct. 21 and inflation at 3.74% in September. The week's dip below 5% is therefore a pause in a high-rate environment, not a return to a low-rate one. Watch the Fed meeting next week, and whether the AI credit worries spread beyond CoreWeave.
articles.wire_headline: 10-year Treasury yield drops back to 5% this week as investors seek cover from AI worries

articles.headline: France Joins the Bond Market's Worry List, Though Analysts Say Not the Sequel Yet
articles.dek: French 10-year yields topped 5% for the first time since 2002 and the gap with Germany passed 170 basis points, but most analysts see a French problem, not a euro zone one.
articles.catch_up: France has a large deficit, a growing debt pile, a weak economy and a shaky political situation. Investors have responded by demanding more to lend to Paris, reviving memories of the euro zone debt crisis of the early 2010s.
articles.why_it_matters: Higher French borrowing costs squeeze the budget of the euro zone's second-biggest economy and could spread to Italy and Spain if contagion takes hold. Anyone holding European bonds, or a euro, is watching the same screen.
body: CNBC reported that France's 10-year bond yield rose above 5% this week for the first time since 2002, then moved sharply higher. The euro has fallen almost 5% against the dollar since the start of the year. Translation: the yield is the interest rate the government pays to borrow for a decade, and investors have decided France needs to pay more for the privilege.

The spread between French and German 10-year yields passed 170 basis points on Thursday, the widest since the euro zone debt crisis of the early 2010s. Translation: a basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point, so the market is charging France roughly 1.7 percentage points more than Germany for the same basic promise. The cost of insuring French debt against default, through credit default swaps, is also the highest since that period.

The worry is fragmentation, which CNBC describes as countries sharing a currency while facing sharply different borrowing costs. In the last crisis, which began in Greece and spread to Portugal, Ireland, Italy and Spain, banks held heaps of government debt and governments were expected to rescue the banks. It ended only after rescue programs with sweeping austerity, and after ECB President Mario Draghi pledged in 2012 to do "whatever it takes" to preserve the euro.

France's case is not subtle. It has one of the highest deficit-to-GDP ratios in the 21-nation euro area, and the government has cut its 2026 growth forecast to 0.5%. Political volatility and social unrest, CNBC noted, raise doubts that anyone can deliver the measures meant to fix the public finances. ING's Carsten Brzeski said, "We are deep into French crisis territory," while adding there is no imminent liquidity problem for the government.

Analysts largely agree this is not 2011 with better lighting. Ninety One's John Stopford said spreads would probably need to be in the 200s before the situation is broadly seen as a genuine crisis, and noted French spreads, though wider than at the peak of the earlier crisis, are far narrower than the extremes in Spain, Italy, Greece and Ireland back then. He also said the market seems to assume things must get worse before EU institutions step in. That is a comforting theory with a slightly alarming precondition.

Forvis Mazars' George Lagarias is the most pessimistic of the group on France itself: he says the country is already in a debt crisis, citing debt of 119% of GDP at the end of the second quarter of 2026, against Greece's 128% in late 2009. Yet he puts the odds of a wider spillover at 10% to 20%. His reasoning is that French debt is worrying but known, and markets can handle known risks. Greece, by contrast, revised its projected deficit from 3.7% of GDP in spring 2009 to 12.5% by October, which is the sort of surprise bond investors dislike.

Aberdeen's Alex Everett called it primarily French risk rather than a systemic euro-area risk, citing stronger banks, greater integration and tools designed to limit fragmentation. He expects contagion to be short-lived. BlackRock strategists were more cautious, calling conditions "materially different" from 2011 to 2012 but saying further volatility and spillovers remain possible.

The backdrop is not French alone. BlackRock pointed to rising government borrowing and AI-related investment pushing up financing costs globally. The latest official data show the U.S. 10-year Treasury yield at 5.13% and the 2-year at 4.81% as of Oct. 21, so France is hardly the only borrower facing a pricey market. Paris is merely the one whose spread has people digging out their 2012 notes.

What to watch is whether the spread heads toward the 200s, and whether Rome and Madrid start paying more too. Until then, the consensus is that France has a problem, Europe has a mechanism, and investors would like to see the first one addressed before the second is tested.
articles.wire_headline: France is flashing euro crisis signals. This time, the fault lines are different

articles.headline: Employers Refuse to Fire Anyone, Also Refuse to Hire Anyone, Call It Stability
articles.dek: Weekly jobless claims fell to 194,000, near a 57-year low, even as payrolls grew by just 29,000 in September and the Fed eyes another rate hike.
articles.catch_up: The US labor market has settled into a pattern economists call low-hire, low-fire: companies keep the staff they have but add few new ones. Meanwhile inflation remains well above the Federal Reserve's 2% target, and markets expect further rate increases.
articles.why_it_matters: If you already have a job, the data say it is probably safe; if you are looking for one, the data are less encouraging. Steady employment also gives the Fed room to keep fighting inflation, which means borrowing costs may keep rising.
body: Initial claims for unemployment insurance fell to a seasonally adjusted 194,000 for the week ended Oct. 17, the Labor Department reported Thursday, according to CNBC. That is just above the 189,000 recorded in the week of July 18, the lowest since September 1969. Put plainly, almost nobody is being laid off, which the economy is treating as good news and a hiring freeze as a separate matter.

Translation: initial claims count people who file for unemployment benefits for the first time in a given week. A low number means few people are losing jobs. It says nothing about whether anyone is being hired, a distinction the current labor market is demonstrating with some commitment.

The hiring side is less cheerful. Nonfarm payrolls rose by only 29,000 in September and have averaged 69,000 a month in 2026, CNBC reported. The unemployment rate rose to 4.2%, though the report attributes that largely to a sharp jump in labor force participation. Translation: more people started looking for work, and not all of them found it yet, which makes the rate go up for a fairly encouraging reason.

Claims have averaged 212,000 over the past year, and the four-week moving average is now 197,750. The layoff rate over the prior 12 months fell to 1% of the workforce, down 0.2 percentage point, while job openings were roughly flat. Employers, in short, have reached a stable arrangement with their workforces: you stay, we do not expand.

Thomas Simons, chief U.S. economist at Jefferies, noted in a client note that claims data suggest stable conditions despite gloomy consumer confidence surveys, headlines about job cuts, and what he called the "phantom job-stealing power of AI." The phrase is worth savoring: the technology blamed for taking jobs has so far not shown up in the unemployment line.

The data matter beyond bragging rights. The week in question is the reference week the Bureau of Labor Statistics uses for its payrolls estimate, so low claims hint at a tolerable October jobs report, due Nov. 6. CNBC also noted the Fed meets next week, and officials have recently described the labor market as a source of strength while worrying more about inflation.

That worry has numbers behind it. Consumer prices were up 3.74% from a year earlier as of the latest reading, against a 2% target, and Brent crude sits at $115.22 a barrel. The Fed funds rate is 3.88%, the 2-year Treasury yields 4.81%, and the 10-year yields 5.13%. Markets expect the Fed to hold in October and raise by a quarter percentage point in December, according to CNBC.

MarketWatch, for its part, headlined its own take on the economy's fourth-quarter start as good, with one big problem: warning signs that consumers will be hit with rising prices. That is the other half of the story. A strong job market is what lets the Fed tighten without much worry about the damage, which is cheerful for the labor statistics and less so for anyone with a variable-rate loan.
Watch the Fed next week and the jobs report on Nov. 6. If employers keep not firing people, the central bank will keep not worrying about it.
articles.wire_headline: Jobless claims near the lowest since the 1960s as low-fire trend continues

articles.headline: Trump's Economic Approval Hits Record Low, Uniting Americans Mostly Around Disliking Groceries
articles.dek: CNBC's latest survey shows 34% approve of the president's handling of the economy, the weakest of either term, with two weeks left before the midterms.
articles.catch_up: CNBC's All-America Economic Survey, released Thursday, polled 1,000 registered voters ahead of the Nov. 3 congressional elections. It found economic pessimism rising, including among Republicans, and a 7-point Democratic edge on which party should control Congress.
articles.why_it_matters: Prices, not policy abstractions, are driving the mood: 80% say prices are rising, and official data show inflation at 3.74% with Brent crude at $115.22. If voters act on that gloom, control of Congress and the direction of economic policy could change.
body: According to CNBC, President Donald Trump's approval rating on the economy has fallen to 34%, with 65% disapproving. That is the lowest of either of his terms, and the survey says the 65% disapproval is the highest for any president CNBC has polled going back to Barack Obama. His net economic approval is -31, which is what happens when you subtract the people who like something from the people who do not and the second number wins by a lot.

The drop is sharp. In July, 38% approved and 60% disapproved, so the president lost 4 points of approval and gained 5 points of disapproval in three months. Translation: net approval is approval minus disapproval, so small movements on both sides add up to a large-looking gap. His overall approval is steady at 40% to 59%, which means voters have apparently decided to dislike the economy specifically and the president generally, in separate compartments.

The more notable shift is within the president's own party. Overall, 63% of Americans are pessimistic about the economy and the outlook, up 1 point from July, but that group now includes 35% of Republicans, up 6 points and the highest of either Trump term. Micah Roberts, the survey's Republican pollster, said the change came "because Republicans have" soured, not independents or Democrats. Eight in 10 respondents rate the economy fair or poor, the highest since December 2023.

The cause appears to be the grocery receipt. Eighty percent say prices are rising, up 5 points from a year ago, and 55% say they are rising faster than usual. Food now worries people more than gas, 34% to 23%, and combined concern about food, gas and housing is the top issue for 57%. For context, the latest official CPI reading is 3.74% year over year, meaning a basket that cost $100 a year ago costs about $103.74 now, before anyone mentions the cheese.

Gas is its own story. Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, sat at $115.22 in the latest data. CNBC reports only 35% say the Iran war was worth it given the rise in gasoline prices, and 46% say it was worth it to disrupt Iran's nuclear development, down from 53% in April. Democrats now lead on Iran by 5 points, compared with a 2-point Republican lead before.

On the ballot question, Americans prefer Democratic control of Congress 52% to 45%, a 3-point gain for Democrats since July. Independents lean Democratic 49% to 33%, and 72% of Democrats are highly interested in the election versus 62% of Republicans. Democrats now lead by 16 points on food and grocery costs, up from 7. Republicans keep an edge on border security and immigration, though it shrank to 9 points from 15.

The one thing that unites the country is corruption. Ninety-three percent say elected officials should not be allowed to own or trade individual stocks of companies with federal contracts, and 89% say companies owned by or invested in by a sitting president's immediate family should not get federal contracts. In 2026, that is about as close to consensus as a national poll can get without asking about the weather.

Both pollsters urged caution. Roberts framed it as a contest between "the map and momentum," noting Democrats would need to flip many districts and states Trump won handily. Jay Campbell, the Democratic pollster, said he does not see a realignment election like 1994 or 2008, but a return to the mean. Translation: the wave may be real, but it still has to cross terrain drawn by someone else.
The survey has a margin of error of 3.1 points, so every number above could wobble in either direction. What will not wobble before Nov. 3 is the price of groceries, which is presumably the point.
articles.wire_headline: Trump's approval rating on economy hits all-time low as midterm looms: CNBC survey
